name: Lingala
confidence_why: The penultimate-stress record rests on one aside in Redden & Bongo 1963, a teaching course that itself calls Lingala a two-tone language and attributes penultimate stress only to some speakers who do not use tone, while Meeuwis 2013 and Meeuwis 2019 describe lexical and grammatical tone with minimal pairs and no word stress at all.
catalog_quote: there are many speakers of Lingala who use a stress system instead of tones. Most speakers who use a stress system stress the penultimate syllable.

tone_statements.citation: Meeuwis, Michael. 2019 [online 2020]. The linguistic features of Bangala before Lingala: The pidginization of Bobangi in the 1880s and 1890s. Afrikanistik-Aegyptologie-Online 2019 (article 5012), 1-43. Koeln: Universitaets- und Stadtbibliothek Koeln. DOI 10.18716/ojs/aaeo/2019_3464.
tone_statements.quote: The evidence shows that the language did not make use of tone distinctions at a tonemic, i.e. meaning-distinguishing, level, neither in the lexicon nor in the grammar. It did fulfill such meaning-distinctive roles in original Bobangi. This functional load of tone was lost during pidginization. (After 1900, during the phases of expansion/extension, Lingala regained meaning-distinguishing tone under the influence of adstrates; but these post-1900 processes of regain lie outside the scope of my contribution.)
tone_statements.locator: p. 11, section 3.2 'Loss of the meaning-distinguishing function of tone', para <39>; also para <90> and <92> (p. 31) on 'the regaining of grammatical and lexical tone' and 'the much more complex tonology.. of today's Lingala'
tone_statements.summary: Present-day Lingala has meaning-distinguishing lexical and grammatical tone, regained after 1900; its pidgin ancestor Bangala had lost the tonemic contrasts of Bobangi.

sources.citation: Guthrie, Malcolm. 1940. Tone Ranges in a Two-Tone Language (Lingala). Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 10(2): 469-478.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Lingala has semantic tones, and many words are distinguished by a difference in tone alone, both nouns and verbs. There is also grammatical intonation, i.e. each verbal inflexion has its own appropriate tone, though there do not seem to be any syntactic tones, as such, to indicate syntactical relationships. There are only two levels of tone, High and Mid. Low tone is never used, as every tone is fundamental, and not affected by neighbouring consonants or tones.
